title: Lesson 4: Speaking and Listening: Planning and Writing 'What the Moon Sees' Poem
objective: Students will plan and write a narrative poem using a model and evidence, while expanding vocabulary and practicing respectful discussion.

what_is_taught.skill: plan writing by discussing ideas with classmates
write a narrative poem using a model and evidence
turn ideas from a planner into complete sentences
use prepositional phrases to add detail
use vocabulary related to time of night to support writing
engage in respectful partner discussion and turn and talk
analyze writing to identify qualities of high-quality work
use writing conventions such as punctuation and spelling

what_is_NOT_taught: Independent writing beyond planning and shared writing

student_actions.recognition_identification: identify vocabulary words and parts of a poem
student_actions.oral_production: discuss ideas with partners and share responses aloud
student_actions.written_production: write ideas on a verse planner and contribute to shared writing
student_actions.reasoning_explanation: explain word meanings and writing choices
student_actions.comprehension_response: respond to questions about the poem and vocabulary meanings

evidence.quote: Tell students they are going to use the Interactive Word Wall protocol again to make more connections between words, grow their brains, and become even stronger readers and writers. Today they will use adjectives that describe the sun.
Using a total participation technique, invite responses from the group: 'What is one connection you made during the Interactive Word Wall protocol?' (Responses will vary.)

Provide students specific, positive feedback about the connections they made between words. (Example: 'Joel, I heard you connect orange with large because at sunrise the sun often looks large and orange.')
Direct students' attention to the learning targets and read the first one aloud: 'I can write a narrative poem using a model and evidence.'
Using a total participation technique, invite responses from the group:
Invite students to turn and talk with an elbow partner as you point to each line of the verse and ask:

For ELLs: Mini Language Dive. Ask students about the meaning of chunks from the 'What the Moon Sees' poem. Write and display student responses next to the chunks. Examples: -Point to the chunk The thin, silver moon. Ask: 'What are thin and silver, and what are they doing?' (adjectives describing moon; details)
Direct students' attention to the learning targets and read the second one aloud: 'I can plan my writing by discussing ideas with classmates.'

Invite students to turn and talk with an elbow partner: 'What do you notice about the information included on the verse planner?'(It asks for the time, what the moon looks like, what the moon does, and what the moon sees, just like the parts of verse 1.)
Tell students that they will first work with a partner to talk about and write their ideas for the 'What the Moon Sees' verse planner for verse 2.
Invite students to turn and talk with their partner:
Dismiss students to their workspaces and invite them to begin writing.

Give students specific, positive feedback on their ability to plan with a partner. ('Example: Ana, I heard you and Danny respectfully come to an agreement about what the moon 'sees' by combining your two ideas.)
Redirect students' attention to the displayed 'What the Moon Sees' poem and reread verse 1 aloud.

Think aloud as you write to model how you use information in the room to help you fill in the verse planner (e.g., the Time of Night anchor chart; Sun, Moon, and Stars Word Wall; Adjectives anchor chart).
Tell students that now that they have helped to plan verse 2, you are going to model how to write it in complete sentences on the 'What the Moon Sees' poem underneath verse 1.

Think aloud and model how to turn the ideas from the verse planner into complete sentences (e.g., 'Midnight. Hmm, I wrote that because it was the time of night. So I write it as a complete sentence: 'It is midnight.' I want to make sure I use a period at the end of my sentence and spell midnight correctly using the Time of Night anchor chart.').
If time permits, invite students to call out the proper letters and words needed for the sentences and model how to use the tools in the classroom to support high-quality writing.
When verse 2 is complete, reread verses 1 and 2 of the poem without interruption to support comprehension.

Give students specific, positive feedback on how they helped to take the ideas from the verse planner and turn them into complete sentences. (Example: 'Kai, you reminded us that the adjectives big and round were describing the moon. That helped me to write the sentence: 'The big, round moon is high in the sky.'')
Remind students that today they learned how to plan a verse of the narrative poem 'What the Moon Sees' and to turn the ideas from the verse planner into a complete verse.
Invite students to turn and talk with an elbow partner:
Refocus whole group and confirm with students that this writing is high quality because it includes details and follows conventions.
Give students specific, positive feedback on their ability to use the High-Quality Work anchor chart. (Example: 'Vinay, you pointed out that using adjectives added details to the writing.')

teacher_actions.direct_instruction: Models how to use a verse planner and anchor charts to write complete sentences for a narrative poem; models use of adjectives and prepositional phrases; models respectful partner discussion.
prompts_that_cue_student_response: What is one connection you made during the Interactive Word Wall protocol?
Using the title as evidence, what do you think this poem will be about?
What do you notice about the information included on the verse planner?
How does our shared writing add to your understanding of how to write a verse for the 'What the Moon Sees' poem?
How do you know that I am writing complete sentences?
